source.title: Pruning Laws for Large Language Models
source.authors: Ayan Sengupta; Siddhant Chaudhary; Tanmoy Chakraborty

record.tranche_reason: It evaluates downstream-task performance on unpruned models at different parameter scales, a different measurement from pretraining-loss scaling. It does not measure held-out cross-entropy scaling or compute-optimal allocation.
record.gate_note: The study's main pruning-ratio results concern performance after pruning, not the claim's pretraining-loss laws; they are not recorded as rows. Table 1 separately reports unpruned downstream performance for models of different sizes, which bears on V6. The study does not fit a downstream performance-versus-size prediction curve.
record.test_reason: The study fits 'pruning laws': post-pruning downstream performance as a power of the retention ratio (1-r) on fixed, already-trained checkpoints. It tests no version of the pretraining scaling claim. Table 1's unpruned scores are the L0 inputs to those laws ('These baseline numbers provide the L0 values'). They come from off-the-shelf models of different families, with no fit, forecast or loss link. The authors' remark that performance 'generally improves with scale' is a passing 'as expected' observation, not a test of predictable downstream scaling.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The main conclusion is that post-pruning performance follows a power law in the retention ratio, with task- and method-specific coefficients, and transfers zero/one-shot to unseen models, pruners and an MoE model. The 'improves with scale' remark is a side note on baselines. The conclusion section states pruning sensitivity increases with scale, while the body says larger models are more resilient.
record.recipe_differences: This is a cross-sectional zero-shot evaluation of downstream task scores across model sizes, not a held-out pretraining-loss sweep over parameters, tokens, or compute and not a compute-optimal allocation study.
record.method_sensitivity: Model family and architecture: the reported cross-family performance comparison does not track size alone.

fits_no_version.finding: Post-pruning downstream performance follows L=L0·P0·(1-r)^α in the retention ratio. Exponents are task-specific (QA 2.42, reasoning 0.22, language 0.73). The form beats seven alternative functional forms on test error (0.05 vs 0.05–0.10). Fit is poor for LaCo depth pruning (adj R2 0.20).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Downstream performance of a trained LLM decays as a power law in the fraction of parameters retained after pruning.

fits_no_version.finding: Pruning-law coefficients fitted on some models extrapolate zero-shot to unseen models and pruners with RMSE about 0.04–0.13. The same form fits a 20B MoE model (α=0.48, P0=0.89).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Pruning-ratio power laws transfer across model families, pruning methods and MoE architectures.

fits_no_version.finding: Larger models (LLaMA-13B, OPT-30B) retain accuracy up to 30–40% pruning. Small efficient models (LLaMA-3.2-3B, Phi-3-mini) degrade at <20% pruning.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Robustness to parameter removal increases with model scale and decreases with training efficiency.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
record.problems: For V6, Table 1 provides cross-sectional category scores but no fitted size-scaling relationship, forecast evaluation, or uncertainty estimates; model family and training differences complicate the size comparison.
record.rows_left_out: No results bearing on V6 were omitted. Pruning-ratio scores and fits were excluded because they measure performance degradation from pruning rather than the claim's scaling behavior.

untested.parts: Pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens or compute.
Extrapolation of pretraining-loss fits to larger runs.
Shape effects on loss at fixed parameter count.
Power laws in other modalities or training regimes. Pruning is post-hoc compression, not a training regime.
No fitted or forecast relation between downstream performance and scale or pretraining loss. Table 1 gives only cross-family baseline scores.
Fit-dependence of pretraining laws. The fit sensitivities reported concern pruning laws only.

record.verdict_notes: Reclassified from tests/T2 to uses_without_test/T4. The OPT series in Table 1 does rise monotonically in average score (0.50, 0.51, 0.56, 0.57, 0.62 from 1.3B to 30B). These are off-the-shelf checkpoints used as L0 inputs, with no fit, uncertainty or predictability test, so they do not test V6's 'predictably'. If a curator wants descriptive same-family evidence for V6, only the OPT average rows would qualify, and at most as weak observed. The LLaMA 7B/13B rows are LLaMA-2 per the setup. Note the internal inconsistency on scale and pruning sensitivity.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens, and compute.
Extrapolation of pretraining-loss laws from small to much larger runs.
Architecture-shape effects on pretraining loss at fixed parameter count.
Power-law scaling in other modalities or training regimes.
The study reports cross-sectional unpruned task scores by model, but does not fit or test a predictive relationship with pretraining loss, nor evaluate forecasts of downstream performance.
Fit-dependence or curvature in pretraining scaling laws; the reported fit sensitivities concern pruning laws instead.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Within the OPT size series and the LLaMA 7B/13B comparison
reader_labels.reason: The authors report generally improving average scores with scale; OPT rises from 0.50 at 1.3B to 0.62 at 30B, and LLaMA rises from 0.64 at 7B to 0.68 at 13B (rows tab1-opt13-avg, tab1-opt27-avg, tab1-opt67-avg, tab1-opt13b-avg, tab1-opt30-avg, tab1-llama7-avg, tab1-llama13-avg).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Comparisons across model families and architectures
reader_labels.reason: Performance is not ordered by parameter count alone: the authors note Phi-3-Mini matches LLaMA-13B's average at 0.68 despite being smaller, while LLaMA-3.1-8B scores 0.69; these are cross-family comparisons rather than a controlled size sweep (rows tab1-phi-avg, tab1-llama13-avg, tab1-llama31-avg).
